32468.e: After the victory over the French troops, General Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared independence on 1 January 1804. He gave the country the indigenous name Haiti.
32468.m: Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared Haiti’s independence in 1804.

32469.q: What contributed most to the failure of Napoleon’s great expedition to Saint-Domingue in 1802?
a: An attack on Paris by the British fleet
An earthquake that destroyed the ports
A mutiny of the whole army
32469.e: General Charles Leclerc landed in 1802 with several tens of thousands of soldiers. Fighting and above all yellow fever wiped out the expedition, and Leclerc himself died in 1802.
32469.m: Yellow fever destroyed Napoleon’s army in Saint-Domingue in 1802.

32470.q: Which structure did Henri Christophe, king in the north of Haiti from 1811, have built to protect against a return of the French?
a: A mighty fortress on a mountain
32470.e: After Dessalines was murdered, Haiti split into a north and a south. Henri Christophe ruled the north as King Henri I and had the Citadelle Laferrière built on a mountain top; today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
32470.m: Henri Christophe built the Citadelle Laferrière in the north of Haiti.

32471.q: In which year did the French National Convention abolish slavery in all colonies, partly under pressure from the uprising in Saint-Domingue?
32471.e: On 4 February 1794 the National Convention decided to abolish slavery. Napoleon reintroduced it in several colonies in 1802; France only abolished it for good in 1848.
32471.m: France abolished slavery for the first time in 1794.

32472.q: What title of honour does Simón Bolívar still have in South America today?
32472.e: Bolívar led the struggles for independence against Spain in several countries. That is why he is honoured as “El Libertador”, the Liberator.
32472.m: Simón Bolívar is called “the Liberator” in South America.

32473.q: Which South American country is named after Simón Bolívar?
32473.e: The former Upper Peru became independent in 1825 and called itself Bolivia in Bolívar’s honour. Bolívar was also its first President.
32473.m: Bolivia bears the name of Simón Bolívar.

32474.q: Which large state was created under Bolívar in 1819 and broke up into several countries in 1830?
32474.e: Gran Colombia covered roughly today’s Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador and Panama. After disputes it broke up in 1830.
32474.m: Bolívar’s Gran Colombia only lasted until 1830.

32475.q: What political goal did Bolívar pursue for the liberated states of Spanish America?
a: A close union of the young republics
A monarchy under the Spanish king
As many small independent states as possible
32475.e: Bolívar wanted to unite the new republics in a strong alliance. In 1826 he invited them to a congress in Panama for this purpose, but it achieved little.
32475.m: Bolívar dreamt of a united Spanish America.

32476.q: In which present-day capital city was Simón Bolívar born in 1783?
32476.e: Bolívar came from a wealthy Creole family in Caracas, today the capital of Venezuela.
32476.m: Simón Bolívar was born in Caracas.

32477.q: What tremendous feat did Bolívar’s army achieve in 1819 on the way to Bogotá?
32477.e: Bolívar led his troops over the high, cold passes of the Andes. He then took the Spanish by surprise and liberated New Granada.
32477.m: Bolívar’s march across the Andes in 1819 is regarded as a military masterpiece.

32478.q: Which other great liberator fought mainly in the south of South America, for example in Argentina and Chile?
32478.e: José de San Martín liberated Argentina, Chile and parts of Peru. Bolívar fought in the north, and the two liberators met in 1822.
32478.m: Besides Bolívar, San Martín was the most important liberator of South America.

32479.q: Against which president, who had ruled Mexico in an authoritarian way for decades, was the revolution from 1910 directed?
32479.e: Apart from a short break, Porfirio Díaz had ruled since 1876. His time brought modernisation, but also great social inequality and land concentrated in few hands.
32479.m: The Mexican Revolution was directed against Porfirio Díaz.

32480.q: Who called for an armed uprising against the government with the Plan of San Luis Potosí in 1910?
32480.e: After a rigged election, Francisco Madero called for an uprising on 20 November 1910. He became President in 1911.
32480.m: Francisco Madero started the revolution in 1910.

32481.q: Which revolutionary leader from the state of Morelos demanded in the Plan of Ayala that land be returned to the peasants?
32481.e: Emiliano Zapata published the Plan of Ayala in 1911. His motto “Tierra y Libertad” (Land and Liberty) stands for the demand for land reform.
32481.m: Emiliano Zapata fought for land and freedom for the peasants.

32482.q: Which revolutionary leader raided the US border town of Columbus in New Mexico in 1916, triggering a US punitive expedition?
32482.e: Pancho Villa, leader of the Division of the North from Chihuahua, attacked Columbus in March 1916. The USA then sent General Pershing to Mexico, but he could not catch Villa.
32482.m: In 1916 Pancho Villa raided a town in the USA.

32483.q: In which year was the Mexican constitution that still applies today adopted?
32483.e: The Constitution of Querétaro was proclaimed on 5 February 1917 and came into force on 1 May 1917. It contained progressive rules on land reform, labour law and natural resources.
32483.m: Mexico’s constitution, still in force, dates from 1917.

32484.q: Which general overthrew President Madero in 1913, who was murdered shortly afterwards?
32484.e: During the “Ten Tragic Days” in February 1913, Victoriano Huerta staged a coup. Madero was shot a few days later, after which new resistance against Huerta formed.
32484.m: Victoriano Huerta overthrew President Madero in 1913.

32485.q: Which party that emerged from the revolution governed Mexico without a break, under its current name, until the year 2000?
32485.e: The party was founded in 1929 as the PNR and has been called the Partido Revolucionario Institucional since 1946. Only in 2000 did a candidate from another party, Vicente Fox, win the presidency.

32486.q: Which barracks in Santiago de Cuba did Fidel Castro attack without success on 26 July 1953?
32486.e: The attack on the Moncada Barracks failed, and Castro was arrested. He later named his “26th of July Movement” after the date.
32486.m: Castro’s revolution began in 1953 with the attack on the Moncada Barracks.

32487.q: Which dictator fled Cuba on New Year’s Eve 1958/59?
32487.e: Fulgencio Batista had come to power in a coup in 1952. After the rebels’ successes, he left Cuba on 1 January 1959.
32487.m: Batista fled from the revolutionaries at the beginning of 1959.

32488.q: On which yacht did Fidel Castro and just over 80 fighters land in Cuba from Mexico in December 1956?
32488.e: The overloaded yacht “Granma” reached Cuba at the beginning of December 1956. After the landing, only a few fighters survived the first battles.
32488.m: In 1956 the revolutionaries came to Cuba on the yacht “Granma”.

32489.q: Which country did the revolutionary Ernesto “Che” Guevara come from?
32489.e: Che Guevara was born in Rosario in Argentina in 1928 and met Castro in Mexico. He was killed in Bolivia in 1967.

32490.q: Which country represented US interests in Cuba as protecting power after diplomatic relations were broken off in 1961?
32490.e: Switzerland took over the protecting power mandate for the USA in Cuba in 1961. It ended in 2015, when the two states reopened embassies.
32490.m: From 1961 to 2015 Switzerland was the protecting power of the USA in Cuba.

32491.q: To whom did Fidel Castro officially hand over the office of President in 2008?
32491.e: Fidel Castro temporarily handed over his duties because of illness in 2006, and in 2008 his brother Raúl officially became head of state. Fidel Castro died in 2016.
32491.m: In 2008 Fidel Castro handed power to his brother Raúl.

32492.q: In which mountain range in eastern Cuba did the rebels wage their guerrilla war from 1956?
32492.e: The hard-to-reach Sierra Maestra served as a retreat for the rebels. From there they spread their struggle to the whole island in 1958.
32492.m: The rebels fought from the Sierra Maestra.

32493.q: On which day did the Chilean military stage a coup against the government?
32493.e: On 11 September 1973 the army, navy, air force and police took power. This ended Chile’s long democratic tradition for almost 17 years.
32493.m: The coup in Chile took place on 11 September 1973.

32494.q: Which left-wing alliance of parties did Salvador Allende, elected President in 1970, lead?
32494.e: Allende won in 1970 as the candidate of Unidad Popular, an alliance of socialists, communists and other left-wingers. He wanted to follow a democratic path to socialism.
32494.m: Allende governed with the Unidad Popular alliance.

32495.q: Which presidential palace in Santiago was bombed by fighter planes during the coup?
32495.e: The air force attacked the Palacio de La Moneda, where Allende was. Allende died in the palace on the same day.
32495.m: The La Moneda palace was bombed during the coup of 1973.

32496.q: Until which year did General Augusto Pinochet remain head of state of Chile?
32496.e: Pinochet lost a referendum on extending his rule in 1988. In March 1990 he handed over the presidency to the elected Patricio Aylwin, but remained commander-in-chief of the army until 1998.

32497.q: Which well-known Chilean singer and songwriter was murdered in a stadium in Santiago after the coup?
32497.e: Víctor Jara was held with thousands of others in the Estadio Chile, tortured and shot. The stadium now bears his name.
32497.m: The singer Víctor Jara was murdered after the coup.

32498.q: Which of Chile’s most important export raw materials did the Allende government fully nationalise in 1971?
32498.e: In July 1971 Congress unanimously decided to nationalise the large copper mines, most of which belonged to US companies. This increased tensions with the USA.
32498.m: In 1971 Allende nationalised Chilean copper mining.

32499.q: In which city was Augusto Pinochet arrested in 1998 on a Spanish arrest warrant?
32499.e: The Spanish judge Baltasar Garzón issued an arrest warrant for human rights crimes. Pinochet was under house arrest in London and was allowed to return to Chile in 2000 for health reasons.
32499.m: Pinochet was arrested in London in 1998.

32500.q: Roughly how long did the Berlin Congo Conference last?
32500.e: The conference met from 15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885 in the Reich Chancellery in Berlin. It ended with the General Act of the Congo.
32500.m: The Congo Conference lasted from November 1884 to February 1885.

32501.q: Which non-European state, besides the Ottoman Empire, took part in the Congo Conference?
32501.e: The USA was represented by a delegation and recognised Leopold’s claims in the Congo early on. However, it did not ratify the General Act itself.
32501.m: The USA also took part in the Congo Conference.

32502.q: Which humanitarian goal did the powers commit themselves to in the General Act of the Congo?
32502.e: The signatories promised to fight the slave trade and promote the well-being of the population. In practice this goal was often used to justify colonial rule.
32502.m: The General Act of the Congo promised to fight the slave trade.

32503.q: Which trade rule did the General Act of the Congo set for the whole Congo Basin?
a: A ban on all trade with Europe
32503.e: In the Congo Basin, merchants from all signatory states could trade without customs duties or special rights. Leopold II later undermined this rule with state monopolies.
32503.m: After 1885 free trade was supposed to apply in the Congo Basin.

32504.q: Which country claimed the mouth of the Congo on the basis of old rights, which helped lead to the calling of the Congo Conference?
32504.e: Portugal referred to its voyages since the 15th century. A British-Portuguese treaty of 1884 on the mouth of the Congo met with resistance from other powers.
32504.m: Portugal’s claims to the mouth of the Congo helped trigger the Congo Conference.

32505.q: What is the phase of very rapid division of Africa among European powers, further sped up by the Congo Conference, called?
32505.e: In the “Scramble for Africa”, almost the whole continent was colonised by about 1914. Only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.
32505.m: The Scramble for Africa led to the almost complete colonisation of the continent.

32506.q: Which statement about the Congo Conference is correct according to current research?
a: It set rules for acquiring territory but drew hardly any actual borders.
It divided the whole of Africa among the powers with fixed borders.
It banned the colonial powers from any further conquest.
It gave African kingdoms a say.
32506.e: Above all, the conference created rules of the game for the colonial powers. Most borders were only fixed later in bilateral treaties.
32506.m: The Congo Conference regulated colonisation but drew hardly any borders.

32507.q: What was the name of the force with which the regime in the Congo Free State enforced forced labour and levies?
32507.e: The Force Publique consisted of African soldiers under European officers. It was responsible for many acts of violence against the population.
32507.m: The Force Publique enforced forced labour in the Congo Free State with violence.

32508.q: In which year did Leopold II have to hand over the Congo Free State to the Belgian state?
32508.e: After international protests, Belgium took over the territory in 1908 as the colony of the Belgian Congo. The country only became independent in 1960.
32508.m: From 1908 the Congo Free State was called the Belgian Congo.

32510.q: Which cruel practice of the troops in the Congo Free State became an international symbol of the crimes?
32510.e: Colonial soldiers had to account for the ammunition they used and often cut off hands as proof, even from living people. Photos of this shocked the public in Europe.
32510.m: Severed hands became the symbol of the Congo atrocities.

32512.q: What did the international protest movement against the atrocities in the Congo Free State achieve?
a: Leopold II had to give the Congo to Belgium in 1908
Leopold II was convicted in court
The Congo came under British rule
32512.e: Journalists such as Edmund Dene Morel and the consul Roger Casement made the crimes known. Under this pressure, Leopold II had to hand over his private colony to the Belgian state in 1908.
32512.m: International protest ended Leopold’s private colony in 1908.

32513.q: Which story by Joseph Conrad, published in 1899, is set on the Congo and draws on his experiences there?
32513.e: In 1890 Joseph Conrad worked as captain of a river steamer on the Congo. In “Heart of Darkness” he describes the violence and greed of the colonial system.
32513.m: Joseph Conrad’s “Heart of Darkness” is set on the Congo.

32514.q: In which German colony did the genocide of the Herero and Nama take place?
32514.e: German South West Africa largely corresponds to today’s Namibia. The colony existed from 1884 to 1915.
32514.m: The genocide of the Herero and Nama happened in what is now Namibia.

32515.q: In which year did the Herero uprising against German colonial rule begin?
32515.e: In January 1904 the Herero rose up against land theft, the loss of their cattle and their lack of rights. The German conduct of the war then turned into genocide.

32516.q: Which paramount chief led the Herero uprising in 1904?
32516.e: Samuel Maharero called the Herero to rise up in January 1904. After the defeat, he fled with part of his people to British Bechuanaland.
32516.m: Samuel Maharero led the Herero uprising in 1904.

32517.q: How did thousands of Herero die after the Battle of Waterberg in 1904?
a: They died of thirst in the desert because the Germans sealed off the waterholes
They died in a volcanic eruption
They drowned while fleeing across the sea
They died in a flu epidemic from Europe
32517.e: The German troops drove the Herero into the arid Omaheke and sealed off the waterholes. Many people, including women and children, died of thirst.
32517.m: In 1904 many Herero died of thirst in the Omaheke.

32518.q: What did the Charité in Berlin return to Namibia in 2011?
32518.e: Skulls of victims had been taken to Germany, where they were misused for racist research. In 2011, 20 skulls were formally handed over to a Namibian delegation.
32518.m: In 2011 the Charité returned skulls of Herero and Nama to Namibia.

32519.q: What was on Shark Island near Lüderitz in German South West Africa from 1905?
a: A concentration camp for captured Nama and Herero
32519.e: On Shark Island there was cold, hunger and forced labour. A large proportion of the Nama and Herero held there died.
32519.m: The camp on Shark Island was a place of mass death.

32520.q: In which year did the German federal government officially call the crimes genocide in an agreement with Namibia?
32520.e: In May 2021 the federal government stated that, from today’s perspective, the acts were genocide, and promised support of 1.1 billion euros. Many representatives of the Herero and Nama criticised the agreement as inadequate.
32520.m: In 2021 Germany officially recognised the genocide of the Herero and Nama.

32521.q: In which year did the Battle of Adwa take place?
32521.e: The battle was fought on 1 March 1896 in northern Ethiopia. It was one of the heaviest defeats of a colonial army in Africa.
32521.m: The Battle of Adwa took place in 1896.

32522.q: Which Ethiopian emperor led his army to victory at the Battle of Adwa?
32522.e: Emperor Menelik II had gathered a large, well-armed army from all parts of the country. Its victory strengthened his rule and the unity of the empire.
32522.m: Emperor Menelik II won at Adwa in 1896.

32523.q: In which year did Italy under Mussolini attack Ethiopia again, partly to avenge the defeat at Adwa?
32523.e: In October 1935 the Abyssinian War began, in which Italy also used poison gas. Ethiopia was occupied in 1936 but liberated with British help in 1941.
32523.m: Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935 to wipe out the disgrace of Adwa.

32524.q: Over which treaty of 1889 did the dispute that led to war arise, because the Amharic and Italian versions said different things?
32524.e: According to the Italian version of Article 17, Ethiopia had to conduct its foreign policy through Italy, which would have meant a protectorate. In the Amharic version this was only an option, which is why Menelik cancelled the treaty.
32524.m: The dispute over the Treaty of Wuchale led to the war over Ethiopia.

32525.q: What consequence did the Ethiopian victory at Adwa have in the peace settlement of 1896?
a: Ethiopia had to give Eritrea to Great Britain.
Italy and Ethiopia formed a joint state.
32525.e: In the Peace of Addis Ababa in October 1896, Italy recognised Ethiopia’s full independence. Adwa became a symbol of resistance to colonialism throughout Africa.
32525.m: After Adwa, Italy had to recognise Ethiopia’s independence.

32526.q: Which other African country, besides Ethiopia, remained independent during the colonial period around 1900?
32526.e: Around 1900 almost all of Africa was occupied by European powers. Only Ethiopia, which had defended itself at Adwa, and Liberia remained independent.
32526.m: Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent around 1900.

32527.q: Which Swiss engineer from Thurgau was a close adviser to Emperor Menelik II and later an Ethiopian minister of state?
32527.e: Alfred Ilg came to Ethiopia in 1879 and advised Menelik II on technology and foreign policy. Among other things, he pushed ahead the building of the railway from Djibouti to Addis Ababa.
32527.m: Alfred Ilg from Thurgau was an adviser to Emperor Menelik II.

32528.q: In which city was Mustafa Kemal Atatürk born in 1881?
32528.e: Thessaloniki, then Salonica, belonged to the Ottoman Empire until 1912. Today the city is in Greece.
32528.m: Atatürk was born in Thessaloniki in 1881.

32529.q: In which battle of the First World War did Mustafa Kemal become known as a successful officer?
32529.e: In 1915, as a divisional commander on the Gallipoli peninsula, Mustafa Kemal fought off British and Australian landing troops. The success made him famous throughout the empire.
32529.m: Mustafa Kemal became known in 1915 at the Battle of Gallipoli.

32530.q: On which date was the Republic of Turkey proclaimed?
32530.e: The Grand National Assembly proclaimed the republic on 29 October 1923 and elected Mustafa Kemal as the first President. The day is now a Turkish national holiday.
32530.m: The Republic of Turkey was founded on 29 October 1923.

32531.q: In which Swiss city was the peace treaty signed in 1923 that internationally recognised the borders of the new Turkey?
32531.e: The Treaty of Lausanne replaced the harsh Treaty of Sèvres of 1920. It largely fixed Turkey’s borders and set out a population exchange with Greece.
32531.m: The Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 established the borders of modern Turkey.

32532.q: Which city did Mustafa Kemal make the new capital of Turkey in 1923?
32532.e: Ankara had been the centre of the national liberation struggle and lay safely inland. Istanbul thus lost its role as capital.
32532.m: Atatürk made Ankara the capital in 1923.

32533.q: Which code of law served almost word for word as the model for the new Turkish Civil Code in 1926?
32533.e: In 1926 Turkey largely adopted the Swiss Civil Code. Among other things, this introduced monogamy and civil marriage.
32533.m: Turkish civil law is based on the Swiss Civil Code.

32534.q: In which year did Turkey replace the Arabic script with a Latin alphabet?
32534.e: The script reform came into force in November 1928. It was meant to make learning to read and write easier and to orient Turkey towards Europe.
32534.m: Turkey introduced the Latin script in 1928.

32535.q: Which day is the day of remembrance for the Armenian genocide, because hundreds of Armenian intellectuals were arrested in Constantinople on that day?
32535.e: On 24 April 1915 the Ottoman government had Armenian politicians, clergy and scholars arrested in Constantinople. Most of them were murdered.
32535.m: The Armenian genocide is remembered on 24 April.

32536.q: Which political movement governed the Ottoman Empire at the time of the Armenian genocide?
32536.e: The Young Turks, officially the Committee of Union and Progress, had ruled as a dictatorship since 1913. Their leadership planned and organised the deportations.
32536.m: The Young Turks organised the Armenian genocide.

32537.q: Which Ottoman interior minister is regarded as chiefly responsible for the deportations of the Armenians?
32537.e: As interior minister, Talat Pasha ordered the deportations. He was shot in Berlin in 1921 by an Armenian survivor.
32537.m: Talat Pasha was chiefly responsible for the Armenian genocide.

32538.q: Where did many death marches of the deported Armenians lead from 1915?
32538.e: The deportations led through Anatolia into the Syrian desert, for example to the area around Deir ez-Zor. Many died there of hunger, thirst and in massacres.
32538.m: The Armenian death marches led into the Syrian desert.

32539.q: Which lawyer coined the term “genocide” in 1944, partly influenced by the fate of the Armenians?
32539.e: Raphael Lemkin formed the word from the Greek “genos” and the Latin “caedere”. He then campaigned for the UN Genocide Convention of 1948.
32539.m: Raphael Lemkin created the term genocide.

32540.q: Which chamber of the Swiss parliament recognised the Armenian genocide in 2003?
32540.e: The National Council adopted a corresponding postulate in December 2003. Before that, the cantons of Vaud and Geneva had already recognised the genocide.
32540.m: The National Council recognised the Armenian genocide in 2003.

32541.q: Which novel by Franz Werfel from 1933 describes the resistance of Armenian villages to deportation?
a: The Forty Days of Musa Dagh
All Quiet on the Western Front
32541.e: Werfel tells how Armenians escaped to the mountain Musa Dagh in 1915 and defended themselves for weeks. The novel made the genocide known to a wide audience.
32541.m: Franz Werfel wrote about Musa Dagh.

32542.q: In which year was the Sykes-Picot Agreement concluded?
32542.e: The secret agreement was made in May 1916, in the middle of the First World War. It planned the division of the Ottoman Middle East after the war.

32543.q: Which two powers divided the Middle East into zones of influence in the Sykes-Picot Agreement?
32543.e: The agreement is named after the Briton Mark Sykes and the Frenchman François Georges-Picot. Russia agreed to the division.
32543.m: In 1916 Great Britain and France divided up the Middle East.

32544.q: Who made the secret Sykes-Picot Agreement public at the end of 1917?
32544.e: After the October Revolution, the Bolsheviks published secret treaties of the Tsarist empire. That is how the Arabs also learnt of the plans to divide the region.
32544.m: The Bolsheviks revealed the Sykes-Picot Agreement in 1917.

32545.q: Which present-day areas fell into the French zone of influence under the Sykes-Picot Agreement?
32545.e: France received the coast of Syria and Lebanon as well as influence in the interior. After the war it became the mandate power there.
32545.m: After Sykes-Picot, Syria and Lebanon came under French influence.

32546.q: What did the Sykes-Picot Agreement plan for a large part of Palestine?
32546.e: Because of the holy places, part of Palestine was to be administered internationally. In fact, Great Britain later took over the mandate.
32546.m: Sykes-Picot planned an international administration for Palestine.

32547.q: Why did many Arabs feel betrayed by Great Britain because of the Sykes-Picot Agreement?
a: The British had promised them an independent Arab state
The British had promised them large payments for oil
The British had secretly supported the Ottomans
The British wanted to occupy Mecca
32547.e: In 1915 and 1916 Great Britain held out the prospect of an independent kingdom to the Arabs if they fought against the Ottomans. At the same time it secretly divided the region with France.
32547.m: Sykes-Picot contradicted Britain’s promises to the Arabs.

32548.q: In what form did Great Britain and France rule areas such as Syria, Palestine and Iraq from 1920?
a: As mandate powers on behalf of the League of Nations
As trustees on behalf of the UN
As occupiers together with the USA
As protecting powers of the Ottoman Empire
32548.e: The League of Nations handed the former Ottoman territories to the victorious powers as mandates. In this way the plans of Sykes-Picot were carried out in a changed form.
32548.m: After 1920 the Middle East was administered as League of Nations mandates.

32549.q: Which work did Theodor Herzl publish in 1896 as the basis of political Zionism?
32549.e: In “The Jewish State” Herzl called for a state of their own as the answer to antisemitism. The work made him leader of the Zionist movement.
32549.m: With “The Jewish State” in 1896, Theodor Herzl founded political Zionism.

32550.q: What did the UN General Assembly recommend for Palestine in November 1947?
a: Division into a Jewish and an Arab state
A joint state under British rule
32550.e: Resolution 181 of 29 November 1947 provided for two states, with Jerusalem to be administered internationally. The Jewish side agreed, the Arab side rejected it.
32550.m: In 1947 the UN recommended the partition of Palestine.

32551.q: Which two states launched a surprise attack on Israel on the holiest Jewish holiday in October 1973?
32551.e: The attack on the Day of Atonement gave the Yom Kippur War its name. After initial losses, Israel was able to turn the situation around militarily.
32551.m: Egypt and Syria started the Yom Kippur War in 1973.

32552.q: Which British declaration of 1917 supported the establishment of a “national home” for the Jewish people in Palestine?
32552.e: Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour promised British support in a letter to Lord Rothschild. At the same time, the rights of the non-Jewish population were to be protected.
32552.m: The Balfour Declaration of 1917 promised a Jewish national home in Palestine.

32553.q: What do Palestinians call the flight and expulsion of about 700,000 people in connection with the war of 1948?
32553.e: Nakba means “catastrophe” in Arabic. The refugee question is still one of the core issues of the Middle East conflict.
32553.m: Palestinians call the expulsion of 1948 the Nakba.

32554.q: In which war did Israel occupy the West Bank, the Gaza Strip and East Jerusalem?
32554.e: In June 1967 Israel also conquered the Sinai Peninsula and the Golan Heights. The occupation of the Palestinian territories still shapes the conflict today.
32554.m: In the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel occupied the West Bank and Gaza.

32555.q: Which two politicians sealed the Oslo Accords in 1993 with a famous handshake in front of the White House?
a: David Ben-Gurion and Gamal Abdel Nasser
32555.e: The accords brought mutual recognition of Israel and the PLO and limited Palestinian self-government. Rabin was murdered by an Israeli extremist in 1995.
32555.m: Rabin and Arafat shook hands at the Oslo Accords in 1993.

32556.q: Which Arab state was the first to sign a peace treaty with Israel, in 1979?
32556.e: After the Camp David negotiations, Egypt and Israel signed a peace treaty in 1979, and Israel returned the Sinai. Jordan only followed in 1994.
32556.m: In 1979 Egypt was the first Arab country to make peace with Israel.

32557.q: In which year did the genocide in Rwanda take place?
32557.e: The genocide lasted from April to July 1994, about 100 days. In this short time hundreds of thousands of people were killed.
32557.m: The genocide in Rwanda happened in 1994.

32558.q: Which event on 6 April 1994 directly triggered the genocide in Rwanda?
a: The shooting down of the Rwandan President’s plane
An earthquake in the capital Kigali
The withdrawal of all UN soldiers
32558.e: When the plane was shot down over Kigali, Rwandan President Juvénal Habyarimana and the President of Burundi died. Extremist militias began the killings that same night.
32558.m: The shooting down of the President’s plane triggered the genocide.

32559.q: Against which population group was the genocide in Rwanda mainly directed?
32559.e: Hutu extremists deliberately murdered Tutsi, as well as moderate Hutu who resisted. The division into Hutu and Tutsi had been fixed during the colonial period through identity cards.
32559.m: The genocide in Rwanda was mainly directed against the Tutsi.

32560.q: According to common estimates, how many people were killed in the genocide in Rwanda?
32560.e: Most estimates put the number of dead at between 800,000 and one million. That was a large part of the country’s Tutsi population.
32560.m: An estimated 800,000 to one million people died in the genocide in Rwanda.

32561.q: Which radio station stirred up hatred against the Tutsi before and during the genocide in Rwanda?
32561.e: The station RTLM called Tutsi “cockroaches” and openly called for killing. Those responsible were later convicted of incitement to genocide.
32561.m: The radio station RTLM called for genocide in Rwanda.

32562.q: Which Canadian general commanded the UN troops in Rwanda and warned of the genocide in vain?
32562.e: Roméo Dallaire led the UNAMIR mission and reported signs of planned massacres to New York in January 1994. Instead of reinforcements, he was given hardly any room to act, and the troops were even reduced.
32562.m: General Roméo Dallaire warned the UN of the genocide in vain.

32563.q: Which rebel army ended the genocide in July 1994 by conquering Rwanda militarily?
32563.e: The Rwandan Patriotic Front under Paul Kagame took Kigali in July 1994. The Interahamwe, by contrast, were the Hutu militias that committed a large part of the killings.
32563.m: The Rwandan Patriotic Front ended the genocide in 1994.

32564.q: In which city was the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda based?
32564.e: The UN set up the tribunal in 1994, and it sat in Arusha in Tanzania. In 1998 it handed down the first verdict of an international court for genocide.
32564.m: The Rwanda tribunal sat in Arusha in Tanzania.

32565.q: In which year was the Dutch East India Company (VOC) founded?
32565.e: The VOC was founded on 20 March 1602 by merging several trading companies. The States General granted it a trade monopoly for Asia.

32566.q: Why is the VOC regarded as a milestone in economic history?
a: It issued freely tradable shares to the general public
It was the first bank with paper money
It was the first to introduce income tax
It was the first state postal company
32566.e: Every citizen could buy shares in the VOC, which could then be sold on. That is why it is often regarded as the first joint-stock company in the modern sense.
32566.m: The VOC is seen as an early joint-stock company with tradable shares.

32567.q: With which goods did the VOC make its biggest profits in Asia?
a: Spices such as pepper, nutmeg and cloves
32567.e: Spices were very expensive in Europe. The VOC secured monopolies on the Moluccas and the Banda Islands, often with great violence.
32567.m: The VOC became rich above all through the spice trade.

32568.q: Which city did the VOC found in 1619 as its main base in Asia?
32568.e: In 1619 Jan Pieterszoon Coen conquered Jayakarta and founded Batavia there. The city is now called Jakarta.
32568.m: Batavia, today’s Jakarta, was the centre of the VOC in Asia.

32569.q: Which artificial island near Nagasaki was for a long time the only European trading post in Japan?
32569.e: During Japan’s policy of isolation, only the Dutch were allowed to trade on Dejima. The VOC ran the post from 1641.
32569.m: On Dejima the VOC was the only European power to trade with Japan.

32570.q: Which settlement did Jan van Riebeeck set up on behalf of the VOC in 1652?
a: A supply station at the Cape of Good Hope
A port at the mouth of the Hudson
32570.e: The station at the Cape supplied the ships on the long voyage to Asia with water and food. It grew into the Cape Colony with Cape Town.
32570.m: Cape Town began in 1652 as a VOC supply station.

32571.q: Over which valuable spices did the VOC wage a brutal war of conquest on the Banda Islands?
32571.e: The Banda Islands were then the only source of nutmeg. In 1621 the VOC under Coen conquered the islands and killed or drove out most of the population.
32571.m: The VOC secured the nutmeg monopoly on the Banda Islands with great violence.

32572.q: When was the VOC finally dissolved?
32572.e: After heavy debts and war losses, the VOC was nationalised in 1796. Its charter expired at the end of 1799, and its possessions passed to the state.
32572.m: The VOC existed for almost two hundred years, until 1799.

32573.q: Trading in which securities gave rise to the first modern stock exchange in Amsterdam from 1602?
32573.e: Shortly after the VOC was founded, regular trading in its shares began. That is why Amsterdam is regarded as the home of the oldest modern stock exchange.
32573.m: The Amsterdam stock exchange grew out of trading in VOC shares.

32574.q: What do you do in a short sale, which already happened with VOC shares in Amsterdam in 1609?
a: You sell shares you do not yet own and bet on falling prices
You buy shares on credit and bet on rising prices
You sell shares back to the company itself
32574.e: In 1609 the merchant Isaac Le Maire sold VOC shares for future delivery that he did not yet own. If prices fell, he could buy them more cheaply later and keep the difference.
32574.m: Anyone who sells short is betting on falling prices.

32575.q: Which public bank was founded in Amsterdam in 1609 to bring order to payments?
32575.e: The Amsterdamsche Wisselbank accepted coins of various origins and kept accounts in a stable unit of account. In this way it made international trade easier.
32575.m: The Amsterdam Exchange Bank of 1609 stabilised payments in the trading city.

32576.q: What did Joseph de la Vega write about in 1688 in one of the oldest books of its kind?
a: Share trading on the Amsterdam stock exchange
The voyage to the East Indies
The wars of religion in France
The building of the Amsterdam canals
32576.e: In “Confusión de Confusiones”, Joseph de la Vega described the dealings on the Amsterdam stock exchange in the form of a dialogue. He already described options, futures and speculation.
32576.m: In 1688 Joseph de la Vega was the first to describe stock exchange trading in detail.

32577.q: For what purpose was a separate building, one of the first of its kind, opened in Amsterdam in 1611?
a: For regular trading in goods and shares
For the meetings of the States General
32577.e: The exchange building on the Rokin, designed by Hendrick de Keyser, had an open courtyard with colonnades. Traders met there at fixed times.
32577.m: In 1611 Amsterdam got one of the first permanent stock exchange buildings.

32578.q: Which European group of stock exchanges has the Amsterdam stock exchange belonged to since 2000?
32578.e: In 2000 the stock exchanges of Amsterdam, Paris and Brussels merged to form Euronext. The main Amsterdam index is called the AEX.
32578.m: The Amsterdam stock exchange is now part of Euronext.

32579.q: What is the famous stock exchange building in Amsterdam, built from 1898 to 1903, called?
32579.e: Hendrik Petrus Berlage designed the building with clear brick forms. It is regarded as an important building of early modernism in the Netherlands.
32579.m: The Beurs van Berlage is a landmark of Amsterdam’s stock exchange history.

32580.q: In which year did tulip mania in the Netherlands collapse?
32580.e: In early February 1637, suddenly no buyers turned up at an auction in Haarlem. After that, the prices of tulip bulbs fell quickly.

32581.q: Which tulip variety was considered the most expensive and most famous of tulip mania?
32581.e: Prices of several thousand guilders were quoted for a single Semper Augustus bulb. The variety had white flowers with red flames.
32581.m: The Semper Augustus was the most sought-after tulip of the mania.

32582.q: What caused the prized flamed patterns on some tulips?
a: A special fertiliser made from ash
32582.e: The tulip mosaic virus breaks the colour of the flower into stripes. This made the bulbs weaker and they multiplied more slowly, which made them even rarer.
32582.m: The flamed tulips owed their pattern to a viral disease.

32583.q: What was the trade in tulip bulbs that were still in the ground and would only be delivered later called?
32583.e: People traded promises of delivery, not the bulbs themselves. These futures deals were often made in taverns and were hardly controlled.
32583.m: In the wind trade, promises were traded instead of real tulips.

32584.q: From which empire did the tulip reach Europe in the 16th century?
32584.e: Tulips were very popular at the Ottoman court. Envoys and botanists brought bulbs to Central Europe and the Netherlands.
32584.m: The tulip came to Europe from the Ottoman Empire.

32585.q: Why is tulip mania considered an early example of a speculative bubble?
a: Prices rose far above the real use value and then suddenly collapsed
The state set fixed maximum prices for tulips
Tulips were introduced as a means of paying taxes
The harvest failed completely for several years
32585.e: Many people bought tulip bulbs only to sell them on at a higher price. When no buyers came in 1637, prices fell quickly.
32585.m: In a speculative bubble, prices rise without real value behind them and then crash.

32586.q: How do more recent historians such as Anne Goldgar judge the economic consequences of tulip mania?
a: As much smaller than long claimed
As the trigger of the Thirty Years' War
As the cause of the downfall of the VOC
32586.e: Studies of the sources show that only a small circle of traders was involved. There was no general collapse of the Dutch economy.
32586.m: The consequences of tulip mania were exaggerated for a long time.

32587.q: Which French doctor is considered the founder of physiocracy?
32587.e: Quesnay was a personal physician at the court of Louis XV. He transferred the idea of a circulation from medicine to the economy.

32588.q: Which work from 1758 was the first to show the economic cycle in a diagram?
32588.e: In it, Quesnay showed how goods and money flow between the classes of society. The Tableau is considered a forerunner of modern circular flow models.
32588.m: The “Tableau économique” was the first to show an economic cycle.

32589.q: According to the physiocrats, which branch of the economy is the only one that produces a real surplus?
32589.e: Only nature increases value, for example when many grains grow from one seed. The physiocrats called this surplus “produit net”.
32589.m: For the physiocrats, only the land creates new wealth.

32590.q: What did the physiocrats call craftsmen and merchants?
32590.e: In the physiocratic view, craftsmen only reshape raw materials without creating new value. Only farmers were productive.
32590.m: The physiocrats counted craftsmen as part of the sterile class.

32591.q: Which tax did the physiocrats call for?
a: A single tax on the yield of the land
High customs duties on imported goods
A poll tax for all subjects
32591.e: Since only the land produces a surplus, only the land should be taxed. This idea was called the “impôt unique”.
32591.m: The physiocrats wanted to tax only the yield of the land.

32592.q: Which physiocrat tried to carry out reforms in France as Controller-General of Finances from 1774 to 1776?
32592.e: Among other things, Turgot introduced free trade in grain and wanted to abolish guilds and forced labour. He failed because of resistance from the privileged estates.
32592.m: Turgot wanted to put physiocratic ideas into practice and failed.

32593.q: Which Greek word does the term “physiocracy” come from?
32593.e: Physiocracy means “rule of nature”. The economy should follow a natural order in which the state interferes as little as possible.

32594.q: In which year was Adam Smith's work “The Wealth of Nations” published?
32594.e: The book came out in the same year as the American Declaration of Independence. It is considered the founding work of classical economics.
32594.m: “The Wealth of Nations” was published in 1776.

32595.q: Which country did Adam Smith come from?
32595.e: Smith was born in Kirkcaldy in 1723 and taught moral philosophy in Glasgow. He is one of the main figures of the Scottish Enlightenment.
32595.m: Adam Smith was a thinker of the Scottish Enlightenment.

32596.q: Which image did Smith use to describe how acting in your own interest can serve the common good through the market?
32596.e: According to Smith, people who seek their own advantage often promote the good of society without meaning to. The term appears only once in the work, though.
32596.m: The invisible hand is Smith's most famous image for the market.

32597.q: Which example did Smith use to explain the advantages of the division of labour?
32597.e: According to Smith, ten specialised workers together could make over 48,000 pins a day. One person working alone without division of labour could hardly make twenty.
32597.m: Smith explained the division of labour using the example of the pin factory.

32598.q: Which famous philosopher did Adam Smith visit in Geneva in 1765 while travelling as tutor to the young Duke of Buccleuch?
32598.e: From 1764 to 1766, Smith accompanied the Duke of Buccleuch through France and to Geneva. There he met Voltaire several times, whom he greatly admired.
32598.m: Adam Smith visited Voltaire in Geneva in 1765.

32599.q: Which economic doctrine did Smith criticise particularly sharply in “The Wealth of Nations”?
32599.e: Mercantilism saw a country's wealth in accumulated gold and silver and relied on customs duties. Smith, by contrast, saw prosperity in labour and free exchange.
32599.m: Smith set free trade against mercantilism.

32600.q: Which work did Adam Smith already publish in 1759?
32600.e: In this work of moral philosophy, Smith stresses sympathy as the basis of living together. It shows that he did not rely only on self-interest.
32600.m: Before his book on economics, Smith wrote a theory of morality.

32601.q: Which farming system replaced the three-field system with fallow land in England in the 18th century?
32601.e: In the Norfolk four-course rotation, wheat, turnips, barley and clover took turns. This meant no field was left fallow any more.
32601.m: The Norfolk crop rotation made fallow land unnecessary.

32602.q: Why did growing clover in the crop rotation improve the soil?
a: Clover fixes nitrogen from the air
Clover loosens the soil with deep tubers
Clover stores rainwater in the soil
32602.e: Nodule bacteria on the roots of clover fix nitrogen and so fertilise the soil. At the same time, clover served as animal feed.
32602.m: Clover fertilises the soil naturally with nitrogen.

32603.q: Why did English farmers grow more turnips in the 18th century?
a: They served as animal feed in winter
Sugar for export was made from them
They replaced the farmers' bread grain
They were used to distil spirits for the army
32603.e: Thanks to turnips, more livestock could survive the winter instead of being slaughtered in autumn. More livestock produced more manure and so more fertiliser for the fields. A well-known supporter was Charles Townshend, known as “Turnip Townshend”.
32603.m: Turnips made it possible to keep more livestock through the winter.

32604.q: Which invention is credited to Jethro Tull around 1701?
32604.e: The seed drill placed the seed in even rows and at even depths. As a result, less seed was lost and yields rose.
32604.m: Jethro Tull invented a seed drill for sowing in rows.

32605.q: What is the name for turning shared common land into fenced private land in England?
32605.e: In the 18th century, enclosures were often pushed through by Acts of Parliament. As a result, many small farmers lost their grazing rights.
32605.m: Through the enclosures, common land in England was privatised.

32606.q: What did breeders do in selective animal breeding during the English Agricultural Revolution?
a: They mated only animals with desirable traits
They crossed farm animals with wild animals
They fed the animals artificial fertiliser
They kept the animals only outdoors
32606.e: Breeders such as Robert Bakewell deliberately chose animals that quickly put on meat or grew a lot of wool. In this way, sheep and cattle became much more productive within a few generations.
32606.m: Selective breeding made farm animals more productive in the Agricultural Revolution.

32607.q: Which consequence of the Agricultural Revolution helped industrialisation in England?
a: Farm workers who were no longer needed moved to the towns as labour
The nobility gave up its land
32607.e: Higher yields fed more people, while fewer workers were needed in the countryside. Many looked for work in the new factories.
32607.m: The Agricultural Revolution supplied food and workers for industry.

32608.q: How did the putting-out system work in textile production?
a: An entrepreneur supplied raw materials and home workers processed them for wages
Farmers sold their own cloth at the market
Guilds made all goods in workshops
Factories with steam engines mass-produced goods
32608.e: The merchant “put out” raw material and often tools. Later he collected the finished goods and sold them on.
32608.m: In the putting-out system, home workers worked on behalf of a merchant.

a: Rural home working for distant markets before the factory age
The first factories with steam engines
Building up industry in the colonies
The crafts of the guilds in the towns
32609.e: In many regions, farming families made yarn and cloth at home for faraway markets. This phase is considered a preliminary stage of industrialisation.
32609.m: Proto-industrialisation paved the way for industrialisation through home working.

32610.q: Which region of Switzerland was a centre of textile home working in the putting-out system in the 18th century?
32610.e: In the Toggenburg, Appenzell and the Zurich Oberland, many families spun and wove at home for merchants. Middlemen, the Fergger, handed out raw materials and collected the goods.
32610.m: Eastern Switzerland was a centre of home working in the textile trade.

32611.q: Which man from the Toggenburg described his life as a yarn dealer and weaver in a famous 18th-century autobiography?
32611.e: Bräker wrote “The Life Story and Real Adventures of the Poor Man of Toggenburg”. The book gives an insight into rural home industry.
32611.m: Ulrich Bräker told of the life of a poor weaver in the Toggenburg.

32612.q: Which uprising of 1844 made the misery of home weavers in the putting-out system known throughout Europe?
32612.e: The Silesian weavers protested against falling wages paid by the merchants. Gerhart Hauptmann turned the events into the play “The Weavers”.
32612.m: The Silesian weavers' uprising of 1844 showed the hardship of home weavers.

32613.q: Why was the putting-out system attractive for farming families in areas such as the Zurich Oberland?
a: It offered extra income on top of poor farming
It freed them from all taxes
It gave them their own factories
It guaranteed fixed wages for life
32613.e: On the small farms, the yield was often not enough to live on. Spinning and weaving in the living room brought in extra money.
32613.m: Home working was an important side income for many farming families.

32614.q: How was watchmaking in the Swiss Jura organised for a long time?
a: Home workers made individual parts, which an entrepreneur had assembled
Large factories made everything under one roof
Monasteries built the watches in their workshops
The state ran its own watch workshops
32614.e: An entrepreneur, the établisseur, bought individual parts from specialised home workers and had them assembled into watches. This system is called établissage. Only later did watch factories take over.
32614.m: In the Jura watch industry, many home workers worked for one entrepreneur for a long time.

32615.q: Which industries particularly shaped the Second Industrial Revolution from around 1870?
32615.e: While the First Industrial Revolution was based on steam, coal and textiles, electricity and chemistry now came along too. Large companies with research laboratories also appeared.
32615.m: Electrical engineering and chemistry drove the Second Industrial Revolution.

32616.q: Which German company was founded in 1883 as the “Deutsche Edison-Gesellschaft”?
32616.e: Emil Rathenau acquired licences for Edison's light bulb and founded the company. In 1887 it was renamed Allgemeine Elektricitäts-Gesellschaft.
32616.m: AEG grew out of the Deutsche Edison-Gesellschaft.

32617.q: What did chemists achieve with the blue dye indigo in the 19th century?
a: They made it artificially in the laboratory
They discovered it in a plant for the first time
32617.e: Adolf von Baeyer succeeded in synthesising indigo in 1880. BASF brought synthetic indigo onto the market in 1897 and so pushed out the growing of the indigo plant.
32617.m: In the 19th century, indigo could be made artificially.

32618.q: What did the Basel chemical industry start with in the 19th century?
32618.e: Companies such as Geigy, Ciba and Sandoz first made coal-tar dyes for the textile industry. Later they switched to pharmaceuticals.
32618.m: Basel's chemical industry began with dyes made from tar.

32619.q: Which process made the industrial production of ammonia for artificial fertiliser possible from 1913?
32619.e: Fritz Haber developed the synthesis from nitrogen and hydrogen, and Carl Bosch made it usable on an industrial scale at BASF. The process increased harvests worldwide.
32619.m: The Haber-Bosch process makes nitrogen from the air usable for fertiliser.

32620.q: Which event in 1891 proved that electricity can be transmitted over long distances?
a: The three-phase transmission from Lauffen to Frankfurt
The opening of the Gotthard railway
The first telephone line in Zurich
32620.e: Three-phase current was carried about 175 kilometres to the electrical engineering exhibition in Frankfurt. The Maschinenfabrik Oerlikon played a major part in it.
32620.m: In 1891, the Lauffen to Frankfurt line showed long-distance transmission of electricity.

32621.q: Which process by Henry Bessemer made it possible to produce steel cheaply in large quantities from 1856?
a: Blowing air through molten pig iron
32621.e: In the Bessemer converter, the air blown in burns off the excess carbon in the pig iron. This produced steel within a few minutes.
32621.m: The Bessemer process turned steel into a mass product.

32622.q: In which year did Henry Ford introduce the moving assembly line at his Highland Park plant?
32622.e: From 1913, the vehicle moved to the worker instead of the other way round. The time needed to assemble a chassis fell from over 12 hours to about 1.5 hours.
32622.m: Ford introduced the moving assembly line in 1913.

32623.q: Which car model did Ford mass-produce from 1908?
32623.e: By 1927, around 15 million “Tin Lizzies” had been built. This made the car affordable for large parts of the population.
32623.m: The Model T was the first mass-produced car.

32624.q: What did Ford introduce in 1914 to keep his workers and turn them into customers?
a: A 50 per cent share of profits
32624.e: This roughly doubled the wage. The high staff turnover in the plants fell, and the workers could more easily afford a car.
32624.m: Ford's five-dollar day linked mass production with mass consumption.

32625.q: Which concept of “scientific management” was Fordism based on?
32625.e: Frederick Winslow Taylor broke work down into the smallest steps and timed them. Ford combined this idea with the assembly line.
32625.m: Fordism adopted Taylorism's breaking down of work.

32626.q: Which thinker coined the term “Fordism” in his Prison Notebooks?
32626.e: In Fascist Italy, Gramsci wrote about “Americanism and Fordism”. He saw it as a new form of work and society.
32626.m: Antonio Gramsci gave Fordism its name.

32627.q: Which 1936 Charlie Chaplin film makes fun of assembly line work?
32627.e: Chaplin plays a worker who tightens bolts on the assembly line and finally ends up inside the machine. The film shows how monotonous the work is.
32627.m: “Modern Times” shows the dark side of assembly line work.

32628.q: Apart from the assembly line, what characterises Fordism as an economic model?
a: Mass production of standardised goods and mass consumption
Doing without machines and paid labour
32628.e: Large numbers lowered the cost per item, and higher wages created purchasing power. This model shaped the industrialised countries until the 1970s.
32628.m: Fordism links mass production with mass consumption.

32629.q: In which city did the stock market crash that triggered the Panic of 1873 (Gründerkrach) begin on 9 May 1873?
32629.e: Share prices on the Vienna stock exchange collapsed after a period of wild speculation. The day went down in history as “Black Friday”.
32629.m: The Gründerkrach began on the Vienna stock exchange in May 1873.

32630.q: Which payments by France fuelled the founding boom in the German Empire after 1871?
a: Loans for building the Suez Canal
32630.e: After the Franco-Prussian War, France had to pay high reparations under the Treaty of Frankfurt. The large amount of money flowed into speculation and new companies.
32630.m: French reparations set off a founding boom after 1871.

32631.q: Which World Exhibition took place in the year of the Gründerkrach?
32631.e: The Vienna World Exhibition opened on 1 May 1873. A few days later the stock market crashed, and the expected numbers of visitors never came.
32631.m: The Gründerkrach overshadowed the Vienna World Exhibition of 1873.

32632.q: What is the long period of weak growth and falling prices after 1873 called?
32632.e: The period up to about 1896 is often called the Great or Long Depression. Prices fell, but industrial production partly kept growing.
32632.m: After 1873 came a long period of economic slump.

32633.q: With which economic policy did Bismarck respond in 1879 to the crisis after the Gründerkrach?
a: With protective tariffs on grain and iron
32633.e: Farmers and heavy industry demanded protection from cheap foreign competition. The tariff of 1879 ended the free trade period in the German Empire.
32633.m: After the Gründerkrach, Bismarck relied on protective tariffs.

32634.q: What triggered a stock market panic in the USA in September 1873?
a: The collapse of a bank that had overstretched itself on railway building
A huge fire in New York
32634.e: The bank Jay Cooke & Company had overstretched itself financing the Northern Pacific Railway. Its collapse led to the temporary closure of the New York Stock Exchange.
32634.m: In the USA too, a bank collapse set off a crisis in 1873.

32635.q: What was an important cause of the Gründerkrach?
a: A speculative bubble with overvalued new joint-stock companies
A failed harvest all over Europe
A war between Austria and Russia
32635.e: After company law was relaxed, countless companies were founded, often with inflated valuations. When confidence faded, share prices fell sharply.
32635.m: The Gründerkrach followed a speculative bubble in shares.

32636.q: What does a gold standard mean for a currency?
a: The currency can be exchanged for gold at a fixed rate
All coins are made of pure gold
Gold is banned as a means of payment
The price of gold is set anew every day
32636.e: The central bank guarantees to exchange banknotes for gold at a fixed rate. This ties the amount of money to the gold reserves.
32636.m: Under the gold standard, money is tied to a fixed value in gold.

32637.q: Which country was the first to move to the gold standard in the 18th and early 19th centuries?
32637.e: As Master of the Mint, Isaac Newton set a gold price in 1717 that in practice led Great Britain to the gold standard. It was introduced by law in 1816.
32637.m: Great Britain was the pioneer of the gold standard.

32638.q: With what means did the German Empire switch to the gold standard in the 1870s?
32638.e: The reparations after the war of 1870/71 made it possible to buy gold. The new mark replaced the various silver currencies.
32638.m: From the 1870s, the German Empire's mark was based on gold.

32639.q: When did the legal link between the Swiss franc and gold end?
32639.e: The link to gold was removed by the new Currency Act, which came into force on 1 May 2000. The new Federal Constitution of 1999 had paved the way for this.
32639.m: The franc lost its legal link to gold in 2000.

32640.q: Which event ended the period of the classical gold standard?
a: The outbreak of the First World War in 1914
The founding of the UN in 1945
32640.e: The countries at war dropped the duty to exchange money for gold so they could finance the war with new money. Later attempts to return to it did not last long.
32640.m: The First World War ended the classical gold standard.

32641.q: In which year did Great Britain give up the gold standard during the Great Depression?
32641.e: Great Britain had returned to the gold standard in 1925 under Chancellor of the Exchequer Winston Churchill. In September 1931, it had to give it up again after capital flowed out of the country.
32641.m: Great Britain left the gold standard in 1931.

32642.q: Which Scottish philosopher described in 1752 how flows of gold between countries automatically balance trade?
32642.e: According to Hume, an outflow of gold lowers prices at home, which makes exports cheaper and brings gold back into the country. This is called the price-specie flow mechanism.
32642.m: David Hume explained the balancing mechanism of gold.

32643.q: In which country is Bretton Woods, where the currency conference took place in 1944?
32643.e: The conference took place in July 1944 in a hotel in Bretton Woods in the state of New Hampshire. Delegates from 44 countries took part.
32643.m: The Bretton Woods conference met in the USA in 1944.

32644.q: At what fixed price was the US dollar tied to gold in the Bretton Woods system?
32644.e: The USA promised to exchange dollars held by foreign central banks for gold at this price. The other currencies had fixed exchange rates to the dollar.
32644.m: In the Bretton Woods system, an ounce of gold cost 35 dollars.

32645.q: Which two organisations were agreed on at the Bretton Woods conference?
a: International Monetary Fund and World Bank
32645.e: The International Monetary Fund was to help with balance of payments problems, and the World Bank was to finance reconstruction. Both have their headquarters in Washington.
32645.m: The IMF and the World Bank were created at Bretton Woods.

32646.q: Which British economist represented his country at Bretton Woods and proposed a world currency called the bancor?
32646.e: Keynes wanted to create an international unit of account. However, it was largely the plan of the American Harry Dexter White, with the dollar at the centre, that won.
32646.m: At Bretton Woods, Keynes proposed the bancor as a world currency.

32647.q: Which US president ended the duty to exchange dollars for gold in 1971?
32647.e: On 15 August 1971, Nixon closed the “gold window”. This “Nixon shock” began the end of the Bretton Woods system.
32647.m: The Nixon shock of 1971 ended the dollar's link to gold.

32648.q: What built-in weakness did the Bretton Woods system have?
a: The more dollars the world needed, the less the gold reserves covered them
It had no fixed exchange rates at all
Only European currencies were tied to gold
The USA was not allowed to send dollars abroad
32648.e: In 1960, the economist Robert Triffin showed that the USA had to run deficits to supply the world with dollars. The more dollars were in circulation, the less they were covered by gold.
32648.m: The Triffin dilemma describes the built-in weakness of Bretton Woods.

32649.q: When did Switzerland join the International Monetary Fund?
32649.e: Voters approved joining the IMF and the World Bank in a popular vote in May 1992. Before that, Switzerland had only taken part in the Bretton Woods system indirectly.
32649.m: Switzerland has been a member of the IMF since 1992.

32650.q: Which war triggered the first oil crisis in October 1973?
32650.e: Egypt and Syria attacked Israel. Arab oil states then cut production and imposed an embargo on countries supporting Israel.
32650.m: The oil crisis of 1973 followed the Yom Kippur War.

32651.q: How many car-free Sundays did the Federal Council order at the end of 1973 because of the oil crisis?
32651.e: In November and December 1973, the roads were closed to cars on three Sundays. Many people used them for walking, cycling or roller skating.
32651.m: Switzerland had three car-free Sundays in 1973.

32652.q: In 1973/74 the oil price rose from about 3 to about 12 dollars per barrel. By what percentage did it rise?
32652.e: The increase is 12 minus 3, which is 9 dollars. 9 divided by 3 is 3, so 300 per cent; the price therefore quadrupled.
32652.m: Quadrupling is the same as an increase of 300 per cent.

32653.q: Which organisation of oil-producing states was founded in Baghdad in 1960?
32653.e: The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries was meant to coordinate its members' oil policies. Its headquarters are now in Vienna.
32653.m: OPEC was founded in Baghdad in 1960.

32654.q: What is the combination of stagnation and high inflation that hit many industrialised countries after 1973 called?
32654.e: Expensive energy pushed prices up while production and employment fell. The usual recipes of economic policy hardly worked.
32654.m: Stagflation combines a stagnant economy with rising prices.

32655.q: How many litres does a barrel, the usual unit of measurement for crude oil, hold?
32655.e: An American oil barrel holds 42 gallons, which is about 159 litres. Oil prices are still given in dollars per barrel today.
32655.m: A barrel of crude oil holds about 159 litres.

32656.q: Which organisation did the industrialised countries found in 1974 in response to the oil crisis?
32656.e: The IEA was meant to secure its members' energy supply, for example through shared emergency stocks. Switzerland is one of the founding members.
32656.m: The IEA was founded in 1974 as a response to the oil crisis.

32657.q: From when to when was Margaret Thatcher British Prime Minister?
32657.e: Thatcher was the first woman in this office. Her policy of privatisation and deregulation became known as Thatcherism.
32657.m: Margaret Thatcher governed Great Britain from 1979 to 1990.

32658.q: What is the economic policy of US President Ronald Reagan called?
32658.e: Reagan relied on tax cuts, deregulation and a tight monetary policy. At the same time, defence spending and the budget deficit rose.
32658.m: Reagan's economic policy is called Reaganomics.

32659.q: Where was the Mont Pelerin Society, an important network of neoliberal thinkers, founded in 1947?
32659.e: Friedrich August von Hayek invited economists and philosophers to a hotel on Mont Pèlerin above Vevey. The society still exists today.
32659.m: The Mont Pelerin Society was founded in Switzerland in 1947.

32660.q: Which book did Friedrich August von Hayek publish in 1944?
32660.e: In it, Hayek warned that a state-planned economy leads to a loss of freedom. The book became a key text of neoliberalism.
32660.m: In “The Road to Serfdom”, Hayek warned against the planned economy.

32661.q: Which university is the economist Milton Friedman and his monetarist school closely linked to?
32661.e: Friedman taught in Chicago for decades and received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1976. The Chicago School stressed free markets and controlling the money supply.
32661.m: Milton Friedman shaped the Chicago School.

32662.q: Which state-owned company did the Thatcher government privatise in 1984 with a large share sale?
32662.e: The sale of the telephone company was the largest stock market flotation in the world at the time. Many private individuals bought shares for the first time.
32662.m: The privatisation of British Telecom in 1984 became a symbol of Thatcherism.

32663.q: What is the deregulation of the London financial centre on 27 October 1986 called?
32663.e: Fixed commissions were scrapped and electronic trading replaced the trading floor. As a result, London became one of the most important financial centres in the world.
32663.m: The Big Bang of 1986 deregulated the London financial centre.

32664.q: What was the bundle of neoliberal reform recommendations for developing countries drawn up in 1989 called?
32664.e: In it, the economist John Williamson summed up the demands of the IMF, the World Bank and the US government. They included budget discipline, privatisation and trade liberalisation.
32664.m: The Washington Consensus summed up neoliberal reforms.

32665.q: During which period did the witch hunts in Central Europe reach their peak?
32665.e: The great waves of persecution did not fall in the Middle Ages but in the early modern period. Mass trials took place especially between about 1560 and 1630.
32665.m: The witch hunts were above all a phenomenon of the early modern period.

32666.q: What is the name of Heinrich Kramer's work, published in 1486, that gave a theoretical justification for the witch hunts?
32666.e: The “Malleus Maleficarum”, in English “Hammer of Witches”, described supposed witchcraft and how to act against it. Thanks to printing, it spread widely.
32666.m: The Hammer of Witches of 1486 provided instructions for persecuting witches.

32667.q: Who is considered the last person in Europe to be executed as a “witch”?
32667.e: Anna Göldi was executed in Glarus in 1782, officially for poisoning, but in fact as a witch. In 2008 she was cleared by the Glarus cantonal parliament.
32667.m: Anna Göldi from Glarus is considered Europe's last executed witch.

32668.q: Which test was meant to show whether someone was a witch by throwing the tied-up person into water?
32668.e: Anyone who floated on the surface was considered guilty, because the pure water supposedly rejected a pact with the Devil. The test was disputed even among lawyers of the time.
32668.m: The swimming test was a cruel trial by ordeal in the witch hunts.

32669.q: Which criminal code issued by Emperor Charles V in 1532 formed the legal basis for many witch trials in the Empire?
32669.e: The “Carolina” regulated criminal procedure and also the use of torture. It threatened harmful sorcery with death by burning.
32669.m: The Carolina of 1532 was the criminal code of the Holy Roman Empire.

32670.q: According to today's estimates, what share of the people executed as witches were women?
32670.e: About 75 to 80 per cent of the victims were women. In some regions, however, many men were also convicted.
32670.m: Most victims of the witch hunts were women.

32671.q: In which region of today's Switzerland did some of the earliest witch trials in Europe take place around 1428?
32671.e: In Valais, persecutions began around 1428, in which the idea of a sect of witches appeared for the first time. Western Switzerland was one of the early centres of persecution.
32671.m: Valais was an early centre of witch trials.

32672.q: What characterises the second stage of the demographic transition model?
a: The death rate falls, the birth rate stays high
The birth rate falls, the death rate stays high
32672.e: In the early transition stage, better food and hygiene lower mortality. At first the birth rate stays high, so the population grows strongly.
32672.m: In the second stage, the gap between births and deaths opens up.

32673.q: In the demographic transition model, what is the gap between the birth rate and the death rate called?
32673.e: The difference between the two rates gives the natural population growth. In the transition stage, this gap is especially wide.
32673.m: The wider the population gap, the faster the population grows.

32674.q: Which scholar warned in 1798 that the population was growing faster than food production?
32674.e: Malthus believed that the population grows geometrically, but food only arithmetically. Famines were therefore unavoidable.
32674.m: Malthus saw population growth as a danger to the food supply.

32675.q: Roughly how high must the average number of children per woman be in industrialised countries for a population to stay stable without immigration?
32675.e: This replacement level is a little above 2 because not all children reach adulthood. Switzerland has been well below it for decades.
32675.m: The replacement level is about 2.1 children per woman.

32676.q: Which factor contributed especially to the fall in the death rate in Europe in the 19th century?
32676.e: Higher farm yields, clean water and sewers lowered mortality. Antibiotics only came into widespread use in the 20th century.
32676.m: Food and hygiene lowered mortality in the 19th century.

32677.q: What characterises the late stage of the demographic transition in today's industrialised countries?
a: High birth rate, low death rate
Low birth rate, high death rate
32677.e: At the end of the transition, both rates are low and growth is small or negative. As a result, society ages.
32677.m: At the end of the demographic transition, society ages.

32678.q: What characterises the first stage of the demographic transition model?
a: High birth rate and high death rate
Low birth rate and low death rate
High birth rate, low death rate
Low birth rate, high death rate
32678.e: In pre-industrial societies, many children were born, but hunger and epidemics led to many deaths. The population therefore grew only slowly.
32678.m: In the first stage, high births and high mortality balance each other out.

32679.q: Which island near New York served as the main immigration station of the USA from 1892?
32679.e: Around 12 million people were processed on Ellis Island until 1954. Today there is an immigration museum there.
32679.m: Ellis Island was the immigrants' gateway to America.

32680.q: Which settlement in Wisconsin was founded in 1845 by emigrants from a Swiss canton?
32680.e: Families from Glarus fled poverty and unemployment in the textile industry. New Glarus still keeps up Swiss traditions today.
32680.m: New Glarus in Wisconsin was founded by emigrants from Glarus.

32681.q: Which US law of 1862 promised settlers about 160 acres of land if they farmed it?
32681.e: Anyone who farmed the land for five years became its owner. This attracted many European emigrants to the West.
32681.m: The Homestead Act attracted settlers with free land.

32682.q: Which event triggered mass emigration from Ireland in the years 1845 to 1849?
a: The Great Famine caused by potato blight
32682.e: A fungus destroyed the potato harvest, the main food, several times. About one million people died and millions emigrated.
32682.m: Potato blight drove many Irish people to America.

32683.q: What were the political refugees who went to the USA after the failed revolution of 1848 called?
32683.e: Liberals and democrats such as Carl Schurz fled persecution. In the USA, many of them campaigned against slavery.
32683.m: The Forty-Eighters were revolutionaries of 1848 who fled to America.

32684.q: Which famine crisis after the eruption of the Tambora volcano triggered a wave of emigration from Switzerland in 1816 and 1817?
32684.e: Ash from Tambora cooled the climate in 1816 and harvests failed. There was a bitter famine in eastern Switzerland.
32684.m: After the Year Without a Summer, many Swiss people emigrated.

32685.q: Which port at the mouth of the Weser was an important emigration port in the 19th century?
32685.e: Millions of people travelled overseas from Bremerhaven. Today the German Emigration Centre there remembers them.
32685.m: Bremerhaven was a major emigration port on the Weser.

32686.q: What greatly shortened the crossing to America in the second half of the 19th century?
a: The building of the Panama Canal
The opening of the Suez Canal
32686.e: Sailing ships often took six weeks or more. Steamers covered the distance in a few days to about two weeks.
32686.m: Steamships made crossing the Atlantic faster and safer.

32687.q: What is the middle-class group that defined itself mainly through university education, such as doctors, lawyers and professors, called?
32687.e: The educated middle class (Bildungsbürgertum) drew its prestige from knowledge and culture. The business middle class, by contrast, relied on property and companies.
32687.m: The educated middle class defined itself through education rather than birth.

32688.q: What is the era between 1815 and 1848 that stands for middle-class home life and withdrawal into private life called?
32688.e: Under the Restoration, many middle-class people withdrew from politics into family life. Furniture, music-making at home and cosiness shaped the style.
32688.m: Biedermeier stands for middle-class domestic life.

32689.q: Which middle-class political movement provided all the Federal Councillors in the Swiss federal state from 1848 to 1891?
32689.e: Liberals and Radicals had won the Sonderbund War and shaped the federal state. Only in 1891 was a Catholic Conservative, Josef Zemp, elected.
32689.m: As the party of the middle class, the Liberals shaped the young federal state.

32690.q: Which role model shaped the middle-class family in the 19th century?
a: Husband at work, wife at home
Wife at work, husband at home
32690.e: The middle class separated the man's public sphere from the woman's private sphere. Working-class families usually could not afford this ideal.
32690.m: The middle-class family divided paid work and housework by gender.

32691.q: Which 1901 novel by Thomas Mann describes the decline of a merchant family from Lübeck?
32691.e: The novel shows the decline of a middle-class family over four generations. Thomas Mann received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929.
32691.m: Buddenbrooks tells of the decline of a merchant family.

32692.q: Which musical instrument was a typical status symbol in the 19th-century middle-class drawing room?
32692.e: A piano in the living room showed wealth and education. Daughters often had piano lessons as part of their upbringing.
32692.m: The piano was a sign of middle-class education.

32693.q: Which form of organisation was particularly typical of the social and political life of the middle class in the 19th century?
32693.e: Gymnastics, choral and shooting clubs combined socialising with national and liberal ideas. In Switzerland, national festivals strengthened national feeling.
32693.m: The 19th century was the century of clubs and associations.

32694.q: What did Marx call the rule of the working class in the transition period after a revolution?
32694.e: According to Marx, the proletariat should take power to get rid of the old class order. At the end there would be a classless society.
32694.m: For Marx, the dictatorship of the proletariat was a transition stage.

32695.q: According to the Communist Manifesto, which two classes face each other in modern society?
32695.e: According to Marx and Engels, bourgeois society splits into owners of the means of production and wage workers. Their conflict drives history forward.
32695.m: In the Manifesto, the bourgeoisie and the proletariat fight each other.

32696.q: Which philosopher influenced the young Marx so strongly that Marx reinterpreted his dialectics in a materialist way?
32696.e: In Berlin, Marx belonged to the Young Hegelians. He took over Hegel's dialectics but replaced the spirit with material conditions as the driving force.
32696.m: Marx turned Hegel's dialectics upside down.

32697.q: What did Marx call the value that workers create beyond their wages and that the capitalist keeps?
32697.e: According to Marx, workers receive only the equivalent of their labour power. The entrepreneur takes the extra value they create.
32697.m: For Marx, surplus value is the source of profit.

32698.q: Which newspaper did Karl Marx run in 1842 and 1843 before it was banned by the censors?
32698.e: As editor-in-chief, Marx sharply criticised the Prussian government. After the ban he went to Paris.
32698.m: Marx began his career as a journalist at the Rheinische Zeitung.

32699.q: What is Marx's view of history called, according to which economic conditions shape society?
32699.e: According to Marx, the mode of production determines politics, law and culture. History appears as a series of class struggles.
32699.m: Historical materialism explains history through the economy.

32700.q: What does Marx call the state in which workers become estranged from the product of their work and from themselves?
32700.e: In the Paris Manuscripts of 1844, Marx described how the worker has no control over his product. Work thus becomes a mere duty instead of self-fulfilment.
32700.m: Alienation is a key concept of the young Marx.

32701.q: Who paid the contributions to the German health insurance of 1883?
32701.e: The insured paid two thirds and the employers one third of the contributions. The state did not contribute directly.
32701.m: The first health insurance was paid for jointly by workers and employers.

32702.q: Which law of 1878 was the “stick” in Bismarck's social policy?
32702.e: The Anti-Socialist Law banned social democratic associations and newspapers. With social insurance as the “carrot”, Bismarck wanted to turn the workers away from socialism.
32702.m: Bismarck combined repression and social reform.

32703.q: From what age did workers originally receive an old-age pension under the law of 1889?
